questions.stem: How many **dorsal extensor compartments** are there at the wrist, and which tendons occupy the **first** compartment?

images.caption: Six dorsal extensor compartments at the wrist
images.alt: Cross-section of the dorsal wrist showing six extensor compartments

options.text: Six compartments; first contains APL and EPB
Four compartments; first contains ECRL and ECRB
Six compartments; first contains EPL alone
Five compartments; first contains FCR and PL

questions.explanation: There are **six** dorsal extensor compartments. The **first** contains **abductor pollicis longus (APL)** and **extensor pollicis brevis (EPB)** — the tendons involved in **de Quervain tenosynovitis**. (Compartment 3 holds EPL, which turns around Lister's tubercle; compartment 2 holds ECRL/ECRB.)
references: Netter, Atlas of Human Anatomy — Wrist

questions.stem: A laceration over the volar aspect of the **middle phalanx** of the ring finger divides the flexor digitorum profundus. In which flexor tendon zone (Verdan classification) does this injury lie?

images.caption: Verdan flexor tendon zones I–V
images.alt: Diagram of the palmar hand showing flexor tendon zones

questions.explanation: **Zone II** extends from the distal palmar crease (proximal edge of the A1 pulley) to the insertion of flexor digitorum superficialis (FDS) on the middle phalanx. Within this fibro-osseous sheath the FDS and FDP run together, so repairs here historically had poor outcomes — Bunnell's **"no man's land."** Modern core + epitendinous suture techniques and early active motion have greatly improved results.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Flexor Tendon

questions.stem:
## Flexor pulley system

The flexor sheath is reinforced by **annular (A1–A5)** and **cruciate (C1–C3)** pulleys.

- The **A2** (over proximal phalanx) and **A4** (over middle phalanx) pulleys are the most biomechanically important — losing them causes tendon **bowstringing**.
- The **A1 pulley** at the MCP joint is the site released in **trigger finger** surgery.

Preserve A2 and A4 whenever possible during tendon repair and sheath surgery.
references: Doyle JR. Anatomy of the flexor tendon sheath and pulley system.

questions.stem: A patient reports numbness of the **thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger**, worse at night, with a positive Phalen test. Which nerve is compressed, and where?

images.caption: Carpal tunnel cross-section
images.alt: Cross-section of the carpal tunnel showing the median nerve and flexor tendons

options.text: Median nerve at the carpal tunnel
Median nerve at the pronator teres
Radial nerve in the radial tunnel

questions.explanation: This is classic **carpal tunnel syndrome** — compression of the **median nerve** beneath the transverse carpal ligament. The tunnel contains **9 flexor tendons** (4 FDS, 4 FDP, 1 FPL) plus the median nerve. The **ulnar nerve travels through Guyon's canal**, superficial to the transverse carpal ligament, and is therefore spared.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Compression Neuropathies

questions.stem: A high-energy fracture of the **mid-shaft humerus** injures the radial nerve. Select **all** deficits you would expect. *(Choose every correct option.)*

options.text: Inability to extend the MCP joints
Numbness of the dorsal first web space
Clawing of the ring and little fingers

questions.explanation: The **radial nerve** supplies the wrist and finger extensors, so injury produces **wrist drop** and loss of **MCP extension**, plus sensory loss over the **dorsal first web space**. Thumb **opposition** is a **median** (recurrent motor branch) function, and **clawing** of the ring/little fingers is an **ulnar** nerve sign — neither is caused by radial nerve injury.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Radial Nerve

questions.stem: An elderly patient falls onto an outstretched hand. Radiographs show a distal radius fracture with **dorsal angulation** of the distal fragment ("dinner-fork" deformity). What is the eponym?

images.caption: Colles fracture — dorsal angulation
images.alt: Lateral wrist radiograph schematic showing dorsal angulation of the distal radius

questions.explanation: A **Colles fracture** is an extra-articular distal radius fracture with **dorsal** displacement/angulation, typically from a FOOSH in osteoporotic bone. A **Smith** fracture is the reverse (volar angulation). A **Barton** fracture is an intra-articular rim fracture with carpal subluxation; a **Galeazzi** injury is a radial shaft fracture with distal radioulnar joint disruption.
references: Rockwood & Green's Fractures in Adults — Distal Radius

questions.stem: A young man has wrist pain and **anatomic snuffbox tenderness** after a fall, but initial radiographs are normal. Which statement about the likely fracture is correct?

options.text: The scaphoid is involved; the proximal pole is at risk of avascular necrosis
The lunate is involved; it never develops avascular necrosis
The triquetrum is involved; it is the most commonly fractured carpal bone
No fracture is possible if initial X-rays are normal

questions.explanation: Snuffbox tenderness signals a **scaphoid fracture** — the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Its blood supply enters **distally and runs retrograde**, so **proximal pole** fractures risk **avascular necrosis** and non-union. Initial films are often normal: immobilize and re-image (or obtain MRI/CT) rather than clear the patient. (Avascular necrosis of the **lunate** is Kienböck disease.)
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Carpal Fractures

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man of Northern European descent has a painless **firm cord** in the palm and a progressive **flexion contracture** of the ring finger MCP joint. The predominant cell type driving this disease is:
questions.explanation: This is **Dupuytren disease** — a proliferative fibromatosis of the **palmar fascia** driven by **myofibroblasts** (which express α-smooth-muscle actin and generate the contractile force). It most often affects the **ring and little fingers**, causing **MCP and PIP** flexion contractures. The positive tabletop test (inability to lay the hand flat) is a common surgical threshold.

questions.stem: A new mother presents with radial-sided wrist pain and a **positive Finkelstein test**. Which structure is inflamed?

options.text: The first dorsal compartment (APL and EPB)
The A1 pulley of the thumb
The extensor pollicis longus at Lister's tubercle

questions.explanation: **De Quervain tenosynovitis** is stenosing tenosynovitis of the **first dorsal compartment**, which contains **APL** and **EPB**. The **Finkelstein / Eichhoff** maneuver (thumb in fist, ulnar deviation) reproduces the pain. First-line care is a thumb spica splint and a corticosteroid injection into the compartment; surgical release is reserved for refractory cases (watch for a septum separating the EPB subsheath).

questions.stem: A patient's finger painfully **catches and locks** in flexion, releasing with a snap. Palpation reveals a tender nodule at the distal palm. Surgical treatment releases which structure?
questions.explanation: **Trigger finger** (stenosing flexor tenosynovitis) is a size mismatch between the flexor tendon and the **A1 pulley** at the MCP level. Release of the **A1 pulley** is curative. The **A2** pulley must be **preserved** to prevent bowstringing. Non-operative options include a corticosteroid injection into the sheath and splinting.
references: Green's Operative Hand Surgery, 8e — Trigger Finger
